title: A mechanism-based cure for endometriosis

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a treatment that durably interrupts the biological processes that establish and maintain endometriosis: endometrium-like tissue growing outside the uterus. The goal is lasting clearance of lesions and prevention of their return after treatment ends, without requiring removal of the uterus and ovaries or indefinite hormonal suppression. This remains a research goal; the supplied evidence does not establish that such a cure has been achieved.

Conceptual synthesis: a mechanism-based cure would connect an established disease mechanism to an intervention that changes the disease's course. It need not depend on discovering a single initiating switch; several processes might require interruption. Lesion eradication, relief of established pain, retention of reproductive organs and restoration of fertility are distinct outcomes. A convincing account of the innovation must specify which it achieves rather than treating any one as proof of the others.

significance.text: WHO's fact sheet dated 15 October 2025 estimates that endometriosis affects approximately 190 million reproductive-age women worldwide, about 10 percent of that population. It also recognizes that transgender men and non-binary individuals who menstruate can be affected. The disease causes pain and infertility, and WHO reports an average diagnostic delay of 4 to 12 years. These burdens make a durable cure consequential even alongside improvements in diagnosis and symptom management.

Conditional significance: successful treatment would change endometriosis from a disease requiring continuing management into one that could be durably eradicated in the populations shown to respond. Its direct advance would be sustained lesion clearance without continued suppression or removal of reproductive organs. Reduced dependence on repeated treatment and surgery would be an important downstream possibility, requiring comparative evidence. Better pain medicines, earlier diagnosis and additional hormone antagonists remain useful advances, but alone would not establish the proposed cure.

The impact has important boundaries. Retaining the uterus and ovaries preserves organs and reproductive potential; it does not guarantee restored fertility. Likewise, clearing lesions need not reverse existing scarring or resolve persistent pain, including pain associated with pelvic floor abnormalities. Fertility recovery and relief of established disease-related pain would therefore be additional demonstrated benefits, not automatic consequences of interrupting the disease mechanism. The concept makes no claim to cure every cause of pelvic pain or polycystic ovary syndrome.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is a sufficiently established explanation of the processes that establish and sustain ectopic endometrium-like tissue, coupled to a treatment that durably interrupts them. WHO states that the causes of endometriosis are unknown and that existing treatments do not definitively cure it. It also reports that lesions may recur after successful eradication. A durable intervention must therefore address more than the visible lesions present at one procedure.

Scientific and engineering synthesis: the barriers include distinguishing causal disease-maintaining processes from accompanying biological changes, establishing whether the same intervention can address different presentations of the disease, and reaching the relevant tissue while preserving normal reproductive function. A mechanism that explains initiation may not be sufficient to eliminate established lesions. Conversely, a treatment that clears existing lesions may leave the processes responsible for recurrence intact. These possibilities require separate investigation rather than an assumption that one discovery resolves both.

Lesion-associated somatic mutations are a possible mechanistic lead in the supplied research, which attributes a discussion of recurrent mutations, including genes also altered in cancers, to a 2025 F&S Reviews article. Its text and even its document identity were not verified in the supplied review because no source artifact was captured. The available material therefore does not establish which mutations are present, whether they cause or maintain disease, or whether targeting them would produce a cure. The cancer-gene comparison also does not by itself establish that endometriosis should be treated as cancer.

Clinical synthesis: developing and validating a cure also requires separating recurrent lesions from persistent symptoms. Pain after treatment can have contributors beyond active lesions, while fertility can remain impaired by prior damage. Persistent symptoms after hysterectomy do not, by themselves, demonstrate lesion recurrence specifically after ovarian hormone production has stopped. The supplied evidence does not establish that stronger claim from the earlier research.

current_state.text: The strongest documented position in the supplied evidence is WHO's fact sheet dated 15 October 2025. It states that no existing treatment definitively cures endometriosis, that its causes are unknown, and that treatment aims to control symptoms and limit long-term impacts. Medicines can manage symptoms, and surgery can remove lesions in appropriate patients, but lesions may recur and symptoms may reappear after therapy ends. WHO also states that hysterectomy is not a cure and that some patients retain symptoms. These are dated statements about the available treatment landscape, not evidence that a future mechanism-based cure is impossible.

The supplied research attributes a review to As-Sanie and colleagues, identified there as JAMA 2025;334:64–78, DOI 10.1001/jama.2025.2975, published online on 5 May 2025. It reports recurrent pelvic pain in approximately 25–34 percent of patients within 12 months after hormonal treatment stops, and approximately 25 percent after hysterectomy for endometriosis. No JAMA artifact was supplied, so the validated review could not verify the article identity, publication details, wording, patient populations, estimates or follow-up conditions. These figures are retained as unresolved reports from the research, not established recurrence rates. They concern pain and must not be substituted for measurements of lesion recurrence.

The research also identifies F&S Reviews 2025;6:100098 as discussing recurrent somatic mutations in endometriosis while leaving a definitive causal relationship unresolved. The research reports access to an abstract and no retrieved author list; the source index contains no captured artifact, and the validated review could not inspect the document. Its mutation findings and conclusions consequently remain unverified within this record. Missing access is an evidence limitation, not evidence that the reported findings are false.

Evidence coverage: the supplied review assessed a retained WHO text identified as complete and untruncated, with no reported extraction issues. The source index records retrieval on 1 November 2026, but retrieval does not update the fact sheet's October 2025 content. No freshness search record was supplied, so developments between that publication and 1 November 2026 have not been assessed. The record supports the documented October 2025 treatment gap without resolving its status throughout the subsequent interval.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: a controlled human trial would test a treatment derived from a stated disease mechanism, measuring clearance of established lesions and subsequent recurrence after treatment withdrawal. It would show durable benefit without depending on permanent removal of the uterus and ovaries or continued hormonal suppression. Evidence that the intervention engages the proposed mechanism would strengthen the causal explanation. These are proposed criteria for this innovation, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Durable lesion clearance after withdrawal of mechanism-based treatment

completion_criteria.text: Proposed outcome assessment: lesion outcomes, disease-related pain, reproductive function and safety would be measured separately. Pain assessment would distinguish recurrent disease from persistent pain mechanisms. Fertility outcomes would be assessed in appropriate participants seeking pregnancy, with reproductive-organ retention reported separately from fertility restoration. A claim to resolve disease-related infertility or established pain would require direct supporting results; lesion clearance alone would support a narrower claim.
completion_criteria.label: Lesion clearance distinguished from pain relief and fertility restoration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability and reproducibility assessment: follow-up would extend across a clinically meaningful recurrence period, with duration justified by reliable evidence for the enrolled population. The supplied material does not establish a universal minimum follow-up period or recurrence threshold. Independent replication and assessment across relevant disease presentations would establish the breadth of demonstrated benefit. Finite follow-up could demonstrate durability over the observed interval, not literal permanence, and finite study populations could not establish effectiveness in every patient.
completion_criteria.label: Durability over justified follow-up independently replicated across disease presentations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: evaluation would report adverse effects, effects on normal reproductive function, treatment burden, retreatment needs and the populations in which benefits were demonstrated. A non-hormonal approach could be desirable, but the decisive criterion is durable benefit after treatment ends; a temporary hormonal component would not automatically disqualify it. Absence of all side effects is not a defensible universal requirement. The supplied evidence supports attention to safety and symptom return after withdrawal, but supplies no numerical safety threshold.
completion_criteria.label: Report treatment risks, burdens and demonstrated populations of benefit

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: OBG-02, Manufacture of a functional human oocyte from a somatic cell; OBG-05, Reversal of human ovarian reproductive aging; and OBG-08, A manufactured uterus that supports pregnancy without a donor graft and chronic immunosuppression, overlap with this concept in reproductive goals. They address oocyte production, ovarian aging and uterine replacement, respectively. Curing endometriosis would not establish any of those capabilities, and preserving reproductive organs would not demonstrate restored oocyte quality or uterine function.

Roster-based synthesis: OBG-09, Fertility-preserving interception of high-grade serous tubo-ovarian carcinoma, shares the ambition of treating serious disease while preserving reproductive potential. Its target is cancer interception, whereas OBG-07 concerns durable elimination of endometriosis. The research's unverified reference to mutations in cancer-associated genes does not justify merging these concepts or transferring a treatment mechanism between them.

Roster-based synthesis: OBG-01, Causal control of the human parturition clock; OBG-03, Extrauterine physiological support across the viability gap; OBG-04, In utero reversal of placental insufficiency; OBG-06, In utero molecular correction of fetal-onset genetic disease; and OBG-10, Restoration of the amniotic compartment after preterm membrane rupture, concern pregnancy timing, physiological support, placental function, fetal disease or membrane-related complications. Their overlap with OBG-07 is the broader goal of improving reproductive health through causal intervention or functional restoration. None is a substitute for curing endometriosis, and an endometriosis cure would not establish these separate pregnancy-related capabilities.

unresolved_issues: The JAMA article's identity, publication details, recurrence estimates, populations and follow-up conditions remain unverified because no artifact was supplied.
The F&S Reviews article's identity, authorship, mutation findings and causal interpretation remain unverified because no artifact was supplied.

The recommendation to remove the unverified recurrence figures and mutation discussion entirely was not adopted. They are retained as explicitly unresolved reports to preserve the supplied research detail without elevating it to established evidence.
Developments after the WHO fact sheet dated 15 October 2025 and through 1 November 2026 remain unassessed.
The causal processes that must be interrupted, and whether one intervention could address different disease presentations, remain open scientific questions.
The extent to which a successful lesion-directed cure could reverse established pain or infertility requires separate clinical demonstration.

Appropriate follow-up duration, recurrence thresholds and acceptable safety boundaries require justification for a concrete intervention and study population; the supplied evidence establishes no universal numerical criteria.

brief.title: A lasting cure for endometriosis
possible: People with endometriosis, where tissue like the uterus lining grows outside it, could finish treatment with those growths cleared and kept from returning. The treatment would interrupt the biological processes that sustain the disease, without requiring removal of the uterus and ovaries or ongoing hormone treatment.
why: Endometriosis affects an estimated 190 million women of reproductive age worldwide. It can cause severe pain and infertility, disrupt work and school, and put financial strain on families.
A lasting cure would let people move beyond continuing disease management. It could reduce the need for repeated treatment and surgery while preserving reproductive organs.

sources.showed: WHO describes treatments that manage symptoms or surgically remove growths. It reports that growths can return after removal and that removing the uterus does not cure the disease.
sources.quote: In addition, lesions may recur even after successful eradication, and pelvic floor muscle abnormalities can contribute to chronic pelvic pain.
sources.cited_for: Existing care can treat symptoms and remove growths, but does not establish a lasting cure.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate a treatment that interrupts the disease's biological processes and prevents its return after treatment ends.

sources.showed: This is a review discussing pelvic pain returning after hormonal treatment ends or after surgery to remove the uterus.
sources.cited_for: The review concerns pain returning after treatment.
sources.not_established: Returning pain does not by itself establish that growths have returned or explain how to prevent them.

sources.who: Authors of the review on mutations in endometriosis
sources.showed: This is a review discussing recurring genetic changes in endometriosis tissue and whether those changes cause the disease.
sources.cited_for: Genetic changes in the growths are a possible lead for understanding the disease.
sources.not_established: It does not establish that these genetic changes sustain the disease or that targeting them would cure it.

shown: Doctors can use medicines to manage symptoms and surgery to remove lesions, the abnormal tissue growths. WHO reports that lesions can return after removal and symptoms can reappear after treatment ends. A lasting cure has not been demonstrated.
missing: Researchers have not established which biological processes must be interrupted to eliminate established lesions and prevent their return.
No treatment has demonstrated lasting lesion clearance after it ends without ongoing hormone suppression or removal of reproductive organs.
A cure would still need evidence that it reaches the relevant tissue while preserving normal reproductive function.

milestones.label: Lesions stay cleared after treatment ends
milestones.explanation: A controlled human trial would have to show lasting lesion clearance after a treatment targeting a stated disease process ends. This would establish benefit without ongoing hormone suppression or removal of reproductive organs.

milestones.label: Lesion, pain and fertility outcomes are measured separately
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to measure lesions, pain, reproductive function and safety separately, including pregnancy outcomes where appropriate. This would establish which benefits extend beyond clearing lesions.

milestones.label: Lasting results are independently repeated across disease presentations
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to repeat the benefit across relevant disease presentations, with follow-up long enough to assess recurrence. This would establish how broadly and how durably the treatment works.

milestones.label: Treatment risks, burdens and benefiting populations are established
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to report harms, reproductive effects, treatment burden, retreatment needs and who benefits. This would define the treatment's practical limits.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether one treatment could interrupt the processes sustaining different forms of endometriosis.
Clearing lesions may not reverse existing scarring, persistent pain or infertility.
The follow-up needed to judge durability, acceptable recurrence and safety would depend on the treatment and population.

page.title: Curative treatment for endometriosis
page.definition: A finite treatment interrupts a disease-maintaining biological process and eliminates endometriosis lesions—endometrium-like tissue outside the uterus—without their returning after treatment ends. The uterus and ovaries remain; relief of established pain and restoration of fertility require separate evidence.

goal.need: Endometriosis affects about 190 million women of reproductive age worldwide. Pelvic pain returns in 25–34% of patients within a year of stopping hormonal treatment. In one trial after removal of ovarian endometriomas, cysts returned within two years in 20 of 69 women on no treatment and 6 of 73 taking a continuous contraceptive pill. Lasting remission could spare patients ongoing suppression, including when they wish to conceive. Pelvic floor disorders can still cause pain after lesions are gone.

completion.title: A finite treatment clears endometriosis lesions and maintains clearance after treatment withdrawal.
completion.criterion: A registered controlled human trial meets its prespecified efficacy and safety criteria for anatomically confirmed complete lesion clearance maintained throughout its prespecified follow-up after treatment and hormonal suppression end. The uterus and ovaries remain. Evidence links the response to the targeted disease-maintaining process. The demonstrated benefit is restricted to the tested disease subtype and treatment-free interval; finite follow-up establishes remission over that interval, not permanent eradication.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; provisional operational test because no external definition of curative treatment was found.
completion.basis: The four-society terminology distinguishes symptom recurrence from lesion recurrence and sets no follow-up interval. No external cure standard specifies a treatment-free interval or a required fraction of patients with sustained clearance. In a nine-patient quinagolide study, 35% of marked peritoneal lesions disappeared during treatment. The remaining marked lesions were excised at the second laparoscopy. The randomized QLARITY trial found no significant difference from placebo in lesion-size change over four cycles. Neither study demonstrated complete clearance per patient sustained after withdrawal.

milestones.title: Established lesions in treated mice are smaller than in vehicle controls at P < 0.05.
milestones.criterion: In mice with surgically implanted endometrial tissue, allow lesions to establish for 21 days before treatment. Compare lesion volumes after 31 days of oral oleuropein at 25 mg/kg/day or vehicle. Calculate volume as length × width² / 2. Mean volume must be lower in the treated group under the study's independent two-tailed Student's t test at P < 0.05.
milestones.set_by: Park and colleagues, Baylor College of Medicine; the published oleuropein experimental protocol and statistical analysis. This is a study-specific efficacy test, not a consensus preclinical qualification standard.

milestones.title: A phase 1 trial supports six months of monthly AMY109 dosing in patients with endometriosis.
milestones.criterion: In the randomized, blinded patient cohorts, compare monthly subcutaneous AMY109 at 0.8, 2.0 or 5.0 mg/kg with placebo for six months. The investigators' assessment of adverse events and tolerability must support further clinical testing of repeated dosing.
milestones.set_by: Chugai Pharmaceutical and AMY001JG investigators; registered phase 1 protocol JapicCTI-183841 and its published primary objective.
milestones.threshold_quote: a once-monthly subcutaneous dose of AMY109 (0.8, 2.0, or 5.0 mg/kg) or placebo for 6 months.

milestones.title: A randomised lesion-directed endometriosis trial receives a favourable research ethics opinion.
milestones.criterion: The responsible research ethics committee issues a favourable opinion on a randomized controlled trial in patients with endometriosis whose protocol includes anatomical assessment of lesions after treatment. The opinion applies to the protocol as a whole.
milestones.set_by: North East–Newcastle & North Tyneside 2 Research Ethics Committee; opinion recorded by the UK Health Research Authority.

milestones.title: AMY109 lowers laparoscopic endometriosis severity at week 53 compared with desogestrel alone.
milestones.criterion: In participants with stage III or IV endometriosis, assess severity by laparoscopy using the revised American Society for Reproductive Medicine score at baseline and week 53. Compare the change in each AMY109 arm, alone or with desogestrel, with the change on desogestrel alone. An efficacy claim for either regimen requires a between-group difference favouring that regimen. The registration gives no minimum score difference.
milestones.set_by: Chugai Pharma Europe; ISRCTN15654320 primary efficacy endpoint and comparator. The registered endpoint concerns stage III/IV disease and is not a published cure criterion or a separately validated endpoint for every listed subtype.
milestones.threshold_quote: score assessed by laparoscopy at baseline (pretreatment) and week 53 (posttreatment)

milestones.title: A finite mechanism-directed treatment leaves no detectable endometriosis lesions at treatment completion.
milestones.criterion: Controlled human evidence establishes complete clearance in individual patients at the end of a finite treatment, with the uterus and ovaries retained. Count a patient as having complete clearance only when no lesion of the assessed subtype remains detectable. State the anatomical assessment method and its detection limits. If surgery also removes lesions, establish the treatment's contribution separately.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas; searches of WHO resources, ESHRE's guideline, the four-society terminology and AMY109 registrations found no published complete-clearance threshold for a finite mechanism-directed treatment.

not_found: No external cure criterion specifying treatment-free follow-up duration, required response fraction and permitted lesion recurrence was found.
No published AMY109 phase II efficacy results or curative results separated by the listed disease subtypes were found.
AMY109 phase I full-text pages were blocked; its indexed primary abstract was available.
No statement disputing the value or feasibility of pursuing a cure was found in the ESHRE guideline or the UK and Ireland research priorities.
